title: SQL Mastery
description: Master JOINs, subqueries, GROUP BY, HAVING, query execution plans, and how indexes accelerate your queries.

segments.text: You know how to SELECT and WHERE. But SQL has much more depth. Joins, aggregations, subqueries, and execution plans separate someone who uses SQL from someone who masters it. Let's level up.

An INNER JOIN returns only rows that match in both tables. Think of a Venn diagram — you get just the intersection. If a user has no orders, they won't appear. If an order has no matching user, it disappears too.

LEFT JOIN keeps all rows from the left table, filling in nulls where there's no match. RIGHT JOIN does the opposite. FULL OUTER JOIN keeps everything from both sides. The direction tells you which table's data is preserved.
Here's a practical question. You want all customers and their orders, including customers who haven't ordered anything yet. Which join do you use?
segments.thought_prompt: Which JOIN type preserves all customers even if they have zero orders?

segments.text: Subqueries are queries inside queries. A subquery in the WHERE clause filters rows. A subquery in the FROM clause creates a temporary table. Correlated subqueries reference the outer query and run once per row — powerful but potentially slow.

GROUP BY collapses rows into groups. Combined with aggregate functions — COUNT, SUM, AVG, MAX, MIN — it lets you answer questions like 'how many orders per customer' or 'average order value by region.'

WHERE filters rows before grouping. HAVING filters groups after aggregation. Want customers with more than five orders? You can't use WHERE with COUNT — you need HAVING. It's a subtle but essential distinction.

Ever wonder why a query is slow? EXPLAIN shows you the execution plan — how the database actually runs your query. It reveals whether it's doing a full table scan or using an index, and where the bottleneck is.

Indexes are like a book's index — instead of reading every page, you jump straight to the right one. A B-tree index on a column turns an O of N full scan into an O of log N lookup. But indexes cost write performance and storage.

Don't index everything blindly. Every index slows down writes because the database must update the index too. The art is indexing the columns you actually query on — especially in WHERE and JOIN conditions.
segments.thought_prompt: If a table has heavy writes but few reads, would you add many indexes or few?

segments.text: SQL mastery comes from understanding joins, aggregations, and execution plans. Write the query that's logically correct, then use EXPLAIN to make it fast. Next, we'll explore the world beyond SQL — NoSQL databases.
